title: Jordan’s cooperative reforms show how shared ownership can connect refugee livelihoods, women’s agency, food production, and social cohesion—without removing legal or financial fragility
source_unit: International Labour Organization, Cooperatives as pathways to advancing decent work and economic inclusion: Lessons learned from the PROSPECTS Jordan experience, 2026
geography: Jordan, with refugees and vulnerable host-community members in displacement-affected agricultural and cooperative settings

observations.period: 2019-2024 programme phase; displacement, labor-market and household pressure

refugee_scale.value: Jordan hosted approximately 710,000 refugees registered with UNHCR in early 2024, while a government estimate placed the total refugee population around 1.3 million

refugee_poverty.value: reported refugee poverty rose from 57% to 67% over the prior two years
refugee_poverty.unit: percent of refugees in cited UNHCR socioeconomic survey context

work_permit_cost.value: the report describes a 425 Jordanian dinar annual work-permit fee for Syrian workers plus approximately 113 dinars in social-security contributions after fee reinstatement
work_permit_cost.unit: annual reported administrative and social-security cost

youth_unemployment.value: unemployment among people aged 15-24 in Jordan was reported at 39.8% in 2024
youth_unemployment.unit: percent of youth labor force in cited ILO context

observations.method: ILO case-study and lessons-learned report based on Phase I PROSPECTS Jordan programme documentation, stakeholder contributions, focus groups, and implementation evidence from 2019-2024.
observations.uncertainty: The context figures come from cited external sources and the programme report is not a representative population evaluation; refugee counts, poverty, fees, and unemployment use different denominators and should not be combined into one causal estimate.
observations.subgroup: Syrian and other refugees, vulnerable Jordanian host-community members, women, youth, agricultural workers, cooperative members, and people facing work-permit or childcare barriers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cooperatives cannot by themselves overcome national labor restrictions, high fees, weak demand, childcare shortages, transport costs, or broader macroeconomic pressure; informal participation may still leave workers exposed.

observations.period: 2019-2024 programme phase; policy and institutional conversion

denominator.unit: PROSPECTS Jordan cooperative-policy and institutional intervention

legal_reform.value: PROSPECTS contributed to the National Cooperative Strategy 2021-2025 and the adoption of Jordan’s Cooperative Law 2025

institutional_capacity.value: support strengthened the Jordan Cooperative Corporation through training tools, new institutional capacity, and integration of decent-work dimensions including occupational safety and health and child-labor elimination

inclusion_route.value: the reforms opened space for women’s representation in governance and dialogue around refugee participation and labor-market inclusion

implementation_gap.value: the report identifies continuing needs for implementation plans, monitoring, coordination, financing, and clearer refugee participation rules

observations.method: Documented programme reconstruction of macro policy reform, meso-level institutional strengthening, and cooperative-level support, interpreted against ILO cooperative and decent-work standards.
observations.uncertainty: The report documents contribution and lessons learned rather than a counterfactual impact estimate; formal law and training do not establish enforcement, durable financing, or equal access across cooperatives.
observations.subgroup: Jordanian policymakers, Jordan Cooperative Corporation staff, cooperative unions and members, refugee workers, women, youth, and vulnerable host communities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Institutional reform can create a more enabling platform without changing the bargaining position of small cooperatives or the everyday rights of workers unless implementation and monitoring are resourced.

observations.period: 2019-2024 programme phase; cooperative livelihood, food and community examples

denominator.unit: documented cooperative examples in PROSPECTS Jordan report

value_addition.value: in the report’s Kufrsoum pomegranate example, fresh pomegranates rose from about 0.40 Jordanian dinars per kilogram to up to 3 dinars after improved processing and market development; molasses rose from 2 dinars per kilogram to as much as 10 dinars and reached international markets

water_and_food.value: the same cooperative reportedly secured funding for 215 rainwater-harvesting wells, distributed 600,000 vegetable seedlings during the pandemic, and provided 500 non-repayable grants to local entrepreneurs and small businesses

social_cohesion.value: joint agricultural and entrepreneurial programming brought Jordanian and refugee workers together through training, standardized work agreements, and shared economic activity

rights_and_safety.value: cooperatives raised awareness of labor rights and social protection, distributed protective gear, organized safety training, and in one case connected a mother to support so her children could return to school

observations.method: Narrative and case evidence compiled by the ILO from programme documentation and focus-group or key-informant material; examples are not presented as a controlled impact evaluation.
observations.uncertainty: Reported prices, outputs, grants, wells, seedlings, and social effects are case-specific and may reflect multiple funders, market changes, selection into successful cooperatives, or unobserved support; the report does not establish net income or population-wide food-security effects.
observations.subgroup: Agricultural cooperative members, refugee and Jordanian workers, women entrepreneurs, families facing childcare constraints, farmers, local entrepreneurs, and communities exposed to water scarcity.
observations.counterinterpretation: A successful value-chain example can coexist with weak performance among smaller cooperatives, donor dependence, limited finance, taxation, transport barriers, and precarious or short-term refugee employment.

observations.period: 2024-2026 report and post-programme outlook; participation limits and durability

women_and_youth.value: women’s leadership and participation improved in some cooperatives, while childcare, household responsibilities, transport, and social norms continued to limit access; youth participation remained limited but targeted initiatives created some work and leadership entry points

financial_fragility.value: many cooperatives continued to face limited capital, donor dependence, weak financial literacy, pricing and marketing problems, and unequal access to training

refugee_durability.value: work-permit restrictions, changing fee waivers, short employment periods, and bureaucratic barriers continued to limit stable formal livelihoods for refugees

monitoring_need.value: the report recommends stronger implementation and monitoring, inclusive financing, representative member-based structures, refugee economic inclusion, youth engagement, and institutionalized decent-work training

observations.method: Lessons-learned synthesis of programme achievements, persistent constraints, participant and stakeholder accounts, and recommendations for Phase II.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not provide a long-term follow-up establishing whether cooperative membership, earnings, safety, social cohesion, or women’s agency persisted after programme support.
observations.subgroup: Small and newer cooperatives, refugee workers, women with care responsibilities, youth, agricultural workers, and host-community members with limited transport or finance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cooperative governance may build voice and mutual support even when financial performance is modest, but symbolic participation should not be treated as durable economic security or formal labor protection.

ILO background on cooperatives and the social and solidarity economy in crisis and post-crisis settings.

boundary: This record adds a concrete cooperative-development intervention route connecting displacement, labor-market access, shared ownership, gender and youth participation, food and water capability, and social cohesion. It is a programme lessons-learned case, not a randomized evaluation, representative refugee survey, verified household-income panel, or proof that legal reform and cooperative outputs produced durable security after programme support.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ILO repository record and the 30-page open-access PDF were reviewed for the PROSPECTS Jordan context, policy and institutional reforms, cooperative examples, reported outputs, refugee and host-community inclusion, gender and youth participation, and persistent implementation constraints.
